I am perhaps more confident than scenarios indicating development in other ethics work areas, but I think my understanding of when and how concrete changes in AI systems can help crack open an otherwise difficult mathematical problem within my own lifetime is limited to 1% level. This is because I am not a mathematician, and do not have the intuitive grasp that one would expect from a mathematician to be good at making such a forecast. Even if I were qualified, math proofs are notoriously difficult to predict. For instance, Zhang Yitang's astounding partial result to the twin prime conjecture came out of top experts looking not at all ready to prove that famed conjecture, nor was even wondering how close they were to it until not long before, around 2005. I cannot say whether major mathematical insight into these known open questions, involving strongly formalized assumptions and theorems, are in statistical reach today's and tomorrow's ChatGPT's.

```Simpson's rule is a numerical integration method that is accurate for continuous functions . Suppose we want to evaluate the integral of a function f(x)
$$
\int_a^b f ( x ) \, dx .
$$
One way to proceed is to sample the function at a few points 
$x_0, x_1, x_2,\ldots, x_n,$
$$
\int_a^b f ( x ) \, dx \approx \left( \frac{b - a}{n} \right) \left(f ( x_0 ) + \cdots + f ( x_n ) \right) .
$$
The coefficients in front of each function value are called the coefficients of Simpson's rule. If the coefficients all add up to one, as they do, we say that the rule is (weakly) consistent. If all the coefficients are nonnegative, then the rule is stable. If the rule is both consistent and stable, then it is convergent. Otherwise, the rule is divergent .
